catalog_locator: Forsberg 1992 Section 1.3.2 'Stress', printed p. 9 (ERIC PDF page 10; verified against the rendered page scan); restated in Section 14 'Summary', printed p. 1…
catalog_quote: 1.3.2 Stress. Stress is on the final syllable of the root word, and it does not shift even when a pronoun suffix is attached to the word. A pronoun is never stressed. In the following examples, the stressed syllable is in bold print: eted 'to deliver (someone or something)' Etedu yem ngà. I'll deliver the child. mung 'to go along with (someone or something)' Mungi do. You come along with me. The only exception to this rule are four words which have the e vowel at the end of the word. In these words, the stress is on the first syllable. The examples given are the only members of this class: bede 'but' ngunte 'I don't know' déke 'possibly/likely' yake 'good if' ... [14. Summary:] Another difference is the fact that stress on a root word always falls on the final syllable, a fact which does not change even when a pronoun suffix is added.

new_statements.quote: The vowel similar to the Spanish o is written with an acute accent mark over it, ó, to differentiate it from the much commoner low back vowel written as o. It should be noted, therefore, that in this language the accent mark, ´, does not indicate stress. Stress occurs on the final syllable of the word-base, and is not marked.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog's final-stress rule (final stress), with one added detail: the domain is the word-base, so the rule is base-final rather than word-final under suffixation. Only source opened that actually states stress placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the last syllable of the word-base (root); it is not written, and the acute accent in the orthography marks vowel quality, not stress. Because the domain is the base, a suffixed word (e.g. kuda-u 'my horse') would carry stress on the base-final syllable rather than the word-final one, though the source gives no such example.
new_statements.identity_note: Porter 1977 p. 1 (Introduction 0.1): Tboli of South Cotabato; 'A few phonological variations have been noted in the Tboli language dependent on geographical area. These have to do with shifts in vowel quality and interchanging of the phonemes h and f'; the Ubu north and west of Lake Sebu are Tboli. Forsberg & Lindquist 1955 and the Porter pronoun typescript in the Zorc folder use the older name Tagabili for the same language. The Reid 1971 open page is Ilongot (Kakiduge:n Bugkalut), not Tboli.

tone_statements.citation: Maryott, Alice L. [Lindquist], Vivian Forsberg & Alan Healey. 1959. The phonemes of Tagabili. Philippine Journal of Science 88(2): 225-243.
tone_statements.quote: We consider that the phonemes of Tagabili include seven vowels ...; fiften consonants, ...; accent (rarely contrastive); and at least five contrastive intonation patterns. ... 4.1. Accent. Accent occurs on the final syllable of the majority of word bases. In these cases it manifests itself as stress. ... 4.2. Intonation. Each utterance has one or more intonation units. Though the phonemic status of these units has not been fully analyzed, the contrast between the following five patterns is quite clear. (1, 2, and 3 represent high, mid, and low tones respectively, and 1′ and 3′ represent extra-high and extra-low).
tone_statements.locator: p. 225 sec. 0.1 Synopsis and p. 235 secs. 4.1-4.2
tone_statements.summary: Full phonemic statement: suprasegmentals are accent (realised as stress, mostly base-final, rarely contrastive) and utterance intonation; 'high/mid/low tones' are intonation levels, no lexical tone.

audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim in the ERIC PDF we hold at the stated page, plus the Summary restatement and the independent 1955 corroboration. The deciding source is a 1992 SIL pedagogical grammar by a long-term fieldworker with an explicit stress section; the base coding (fixed final on the root, enclitic pronouns unstressed) is stated three times across 1955/1992 and nothing found contradicts it. The only open question is the framing of the exception: Forsberg 1992 lists four schwa-final function words as the sole exceptions, while the 2004 SIL dictionary (per Wikipedia's citation) reportedly states a general 'final schwa -> penult' retraction; extensionally these may coincide, so this is a possible refinement of the exception field (listed-set vs vowel-quality-conditioned), not a reclassify of the final-stress classification.
